title: Are Chinese Websites Too Complex?
sample: Think-aloud usability testing with 12 participants (6 native Chinese users, 6 expatriates living in China), 2 tasks each on 8 of 14 Chinese sites; small, qualitative
notes: Primary text read on 2026-11-09 (nngroup.com). It reports that Chinese participants tolerate and prefer fairly high information density, especially on portal and news sites, but also hit many usability problems on complex sites and found some too complicated. It does NOT report a general Western preference for simplicity: its foreign participants were expatriates in China, who were less annoyed by problems on simple sites than on complex ones.

title: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2
sample: Accessibility standard (success criteria 1.4.1 use of colour, 1.4.3 contrast minimum, 1.4.12 text spacing, 2.5.8 target size, 3.1.2 language of parts)
notes: Primary text read on 2026-11-10 (w3.org/TR/WCAG22). Criteria read: 1.4.1 (colour not the only means), 1.4.3 (4.5:1; 3:1 for large text; exceptions: incidental, logotypes), 1.4.12, 2.5.8 (24 by 24 CSS px, with exceptions: spacing, equivalent, inline, user agent control, essential). xsuit's guard models the spacing and inline exceptions (B15); equivalent, user agent control and essential are not modelled, so the guard may undo more than WCAG strictly requires. Used only as a constraint on effects, never as evidence of cultural difference. B20: 3.1.2 Language of Parts (Level AA) also read on 2026-11-10: the language of each passage can be programmatically determined; xsuit marks the English text it adds with lang="en".

title: Requirements for Chinese Text Layout (clreq)
sample: Layout requirements for Chinese text (W3C document, dated 4 November 2026 on the page read)
notes: Primary text read on 2026-11-10, section 7.1.1 (type area): the line gap is mostly between 50 % and 100 % of the font size, and line height = font size + line gap, so line-height between 1.5 and 2.0. Written for typeset pages, not specifically for screens. Used only as a constraint on xsuit's typography (line height is never set below 1.5 on pages with CJK text), never as evidence of a cultural difference.

title: Requirements for Japanese Text Layout (jlreq)
sample: Layout requirements for Japanese text (W3C Working Group Note, dated 11 August 2020 on the page read)
notes: Primary text read on 2026-11-10, section on the basic text area (kihon-hanmen): the line gap is often between half an em and one em of the character size, so line-height between 1.5 and 2.0; one em or close to it is more appropriate when lines are longer than 35 characters. Written for typeset pages, not specifically for screens. Used only as a constraint on xsuit's typography, never as evidence of a cultural difference.
